```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

Assigning ages to reporting bands creates categories that you can count, compare,
and carry into an analysis. To interpret those categories correctly, you also
need to know the boundaries behind their labels. A label such as “5 through 9”
is useful for display, but the interval definition establishes exactly which
ages belong.

In Agecraft, an `age_interval` defines the bands, and an `age_group` stores each
observation's assignment together with those definitions. This vignette follows
a small set of observations through classification, subsetting, relabeling, and
combination. Along the way, you will see how interval boundaries determine
membership, why unused categories remain after subsetting, and what makes two
sets of assignments compatible.

By the end, you should be able to work with assigned age groups while keeping
their labels and definitions aligned, and recognize when a change requires
classification again from the original ages. Assignments do not retain the
original exact ages or the provenance of an age scheme, so keep that information
separately when your analysis needs it.

## Assign observations to age bands

Suppose you need counts by age band for a small set of records. Each row below
represents one synthetic observation with an identifier and an age in years.
These bands are illustrative reporting choices, not an external standard.

```{r observations}
records <- data.frame(
  id = paste0("A", 1:5),
  age = age(c(2, 5, 8, 12, NA), unit = "year")
)
bands <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 5, 10, Inf), unit = "year")
records$group <- categorize_age(records$age, by = bands)
records
```

Each assignment corresponds to the age in the same row. Keeping both columns
lets you check the assignment and classify the observations again if the bands
change. The missing age in record A5 has a missing assignment.

## Inspect labels and their boundaries

```{r definitions}
class(records$group)
group_intervals(records$group)
```

An `age_group` is an ordered factor with one interval definition per level.
Its integer codes identify categories; they are not numerical ages. The levels
follow chronological interval order.

The first band is `[0, 5)` and the second is `[5, 10)`: a lower bound is included
and an upper bound is excluded. Record A2, aged exactly 5 years, therefore
belongs to the second band. The final `Inf` extends the third band from age 10
onward. For more on constructing bands, see `help("age_interval")`.

Missing assignments can also mean that the chosen bands do not cover an
observed age. To see the difference, temporarily restrict coverage to ages
below 10:

```{r incomplete-coverage}
under_ten <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 5, 10), unit = "year")
data.frame(
  id = records$id,
  age = records$age,
  group = categorize_age(records$age, by = under_ten)
)
```

A4 has an observed age of 12 and falls outside this definition; A5 has no
observed age. Both assignments are `NA`, so the assigned groups alone cannot
distinguish these causes. Missingness is not a category level.

## Subset records and retain reporting categories

Return to the original three bands. If a report includes only the first three
records, no observation is in the oldest band:

```{r subset-records}
selected <- records[1:3, ]
table(selected$group)
group_intervals(selected$group)
```

The oldest band remains in the definition and appears with a count of zero.
Retaining unused categories lets reports for different subsets use the same
bands, even when some bands have no observations.

If you want only the categories observed in this subset, drop the unused levels
explicitly:

```{r drop-unused}
observed_groups <- droplevels(selected$group)
levels(observed_groups)
group_intervals(observed_groups)
```

`droplevels()` removes unused levels and their interval definitions together.
Use it when the reduced set is useful, remembering that it changes the categories
available for subsequent reporting and combination.

## Relabel categories without changing membership

The original assignments can use descriptive labels while retaining their
boundaries:

```{r relabel}
renamed <- records$group
levels(renamed) <- c("Under 5", "5 through 9", "10 and older")
renamed
names(group_intervals(renamed))
group_intervals(renamed)
```

The interval names follow the new labels, but the bounds and each observation's
membership stay the same. Labels must be unique and nonblank; implicit merging
and level reordering are rejected. Changing a label does not change a boundary.
To use different boundaries, define new intervals and classify `records$age`
again. The original ages are needed because assignments do not preserve the
position of an observation within its band.

## Combine batches with compatible definitions

Suppose two more observations arrive. Classify them using the same definition
before combining the batches:

```{r combine-batches}
new_records <- data.frame(
  id = c("B1", "B2"),
  age = age(c(4, 10), unit = "year")
)
new_records$group <- categorize_age(new_records$age, by = bands)
all_records <- vctrs::vec_rbind(records, new_records)
all_records
table(all_records$group, useNA = "ifany")
```

The combined counts include both batches and show the missing assignment
separately. Combining groups requires matching chronological bounds, labels,
and definition units. Identical labels alone do not establish compatibility.
For example, the relabeled vector above cannot be combined directly with the
original assignments, and the definition reduced by `droplevels()` no longer
matches the full definition.

Use `vctrs::vec_rbind()` to bind records while preserving their group definitions.
Base `rbind.data.frame()` can reconstruct factor columns and discard the
subclass and definitions. To concatenate group vectors alone, use
`c(records$group, new_records$group)` with compatible definitions.

## Convert to ordinary factors when needed

Some display tasks require a different category order. Convert a copy to an
ordinary factor before changing its levels:

```{r ordinary-factor}
plot_groups <- generics::as.factor(all_records$group)
plot_groups <- factor(plot_groups, levels = rev(levels(plot_groups)))
levels(plot_groups)
class(plot_groups)
```

This copy no longer carries interval definitions. Keep `all_records$group` for
operations that need the mapping between labels and bounds.
`generics::as.ordered()` also removes the group metadata, producing an ordinary
ordered factor. Base `as.factor()` and `as.ordered()` return existing factor
subclasses unchanged; use the explicit `generics` conversions when you need to
remove the subclass. Convert all inputs explicitly before combining groups with
ordinary factors or character vectors.

## Understand the units of the definition

The reporting bands above and their observations both use years. When the units
differ, classification can convert the observations to the definition's unit.
For example, a separate infant report might use weeks for ages recorded in days:

```{r definition-units}
weekly_bands <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 1, Inf), unit = "week")
infant_groups <- categorize_age(age(c(3, 8), unit = "day"), by = weekly_bands)
infant_groups
group_intervals(infant_groups)
```

Three days falls below one week; eight days falls in the second interval,
`[1, Inf)` weeks. The retrieved definitions use weeks. When definition units are
unspecified, they inherit the observation unit. Explicit units make the intended
scale clear when a definition is reused.

Day-to-week conversion uses elapsed-time units. Conversions involving calendar
months or years require `allow_approx = TRUE`; for exact calendar classification,
calculate ages from the original dates in the definition's unit. See
`help("categorize_age")` for conversion controls and output choices.

The legacy `units` attribute on an assignment records the original observation
unit, which is days in this example. It does not identify the unit of the
boundaries. Combining compatible groups with different observation units drops
that attribute; the definition units must still match.

## Reconstruct saved objects from earlier versions

Older versions used `age_group` for interval records. Rebuild those definitions
with `age_interval()` before using them. Saved `age_category` assignments need
reconstruction with `age_group(labels, intervals)` using their labels and rebuilt
interval definitions. Changing a class attribute alone does not validate an
object. See the [class naming migration guide](https://github.com/RussJones007/agecraft/blob/main/docs/age_class_naming_migration.md)
for reconstruction examples.

## Carry definitions forward

The examples retained the meaning of the reporting bands through subsetting,
relabeling, and combination. Keep the original ages for reclassification and
retain a scheme separately when its identity and provenance matter. Assigned
groups provide counts for the observed records; rates also require compatible
population denominators.

For a broader view of the representations, see [Understanding ages, intervals, groups, and schemes](classes.html).
To attach purpose and provenance to reusable definitions, continue with
[Creating and using reusable age schemes](age-schemes.html). The full assignment
interface is documented in `help("age_group")` and `help("categorize_age")`.
